<jats:p>We continue here our work on fractional integration and differentiation of functions of a real variable which we began in a previous paper. All quantities in the present paper are real.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    We define a
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    th integral, or a (−
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    )th differential coefficient, of
                    <jats:italic>f(x)</jats:italic>
                    over an interval (
                    <jats:italic>a, x</jats:italic>
                    )by
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S0025557200066821_inline1"/>
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    where
                    <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                    stands for
                    <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S0025557200066821_inline2"/>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    is the least integer greater than or equal to zero such that
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    +
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    >0,
                    <jats:italic>f</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>x</jats:italic>
                    ) is bounded on the path of integration, and is continuous on this path except possibly for a finite number of ordinary discontinuities.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>In a previous paper we considered fractional integration and differentiation of functions of a real variable. In the present paper the complex variable will be used.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    We define a
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    th integral, or a (−
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    )th differential coefficient, of
                    <jats:italic>f(z)</jats:italic>
                    along a simple curve
                    <jats:italic>l</jats:italic>
                    by
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S0025557200065633_inline01"/>
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    where the integration and differentiation are along
                    <jats:italic>l</jats:italic>
                    , starting from
                    <jats:italic>a, λ</jats:italic>
                    is any number, real or complex,
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    is the least integer greater than or equal to zero such that
                    <jats:italic>R(λ)</jats:italic>
                    +
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    > 0,
                    <jats:italic>R(λ)</jats:italic>
                    being the real part of
                    <jats:italic>λ</jats:italic>
                    ; and
                    <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                    stands for
                    <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S0025557200065633_inline02"/>
                    , denoting differentiation along
                    <jats:italic>l. a</jats:italic>
                    is arbitrary and independent of
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                    , and in the present paper is to be taken as finite.
                  </jats:p>
